assertions.text: Table uses value-set syntax (curly braces like {READ, WRITE} or {READ, WRITE, DELETE}) to express rules that hold across multiple actions — rather than one row per role/action combination
Table has fewer than 9 data rows (i.e. does not enumerate every role/action combination individually)
Test method body contains no if or switch statements
Table has a scenario/description column as the leftmost column
No two rows share both the same Role value and the same boolean output — forces value set consolidation (e.g. USER can READ and USER can WRITE, both true, should be one row with {READ, WRITE}).

Test method has either a @DisplayName annotation or a method name that reads as a clear, descriptive title when converted from camelCase/snake_case (e.g. 'permissionsByRoleAndAction' → 'Permissions By Role And Action'). Not a generic name like 'test1' or 'canPerform'.

If @Description is present, it provides context beyond what the table rows already express — such as where permissions are checked in the request lifecycle, or open questions. Does NOT merely restate the column names or summarise what the rows show. It is acceptable to omit @Description if the table already conveys all relevant context.
Annotations appear in order: @DisplayName (if present), @Description (if present), @TableTest — not any other order.
If @Description is present and the text is longer than a single short line, it uses a text block (triple-quoted string """), not string concatenation with +. Passes if @Description is absent.
Scenario names describe conditions ('Admin performs any action', 'Guest reads') — not outcomes ('Allowed', 'Denied').
The build file (build.gradle) includes org.tabletest:tabletest-junit:1.2.1 as a test dependency
The generated test code compiles successfully against the project scaffolding
